title: NEET PG — General Medicine | Hematology Anemia Types
description: Subject-wise test on Hematology Anemia Types (General Medicine) for NEET PG. 40Q.
subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 35-year-old female presents with chronic fatigue, pallor, and exertional dyspnea. Her complete blood count reveals hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, MCV 72 fL, MCH 22 pg. Serum ferritin is 8 ng/mL and TIBC is 450 mcg/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Alpha thalassemia trait would typically have normal iron studies.
The very low serum ferritin and high TIBC are pathognomonic for iron deficiency anemia.
Anemia of chronic disease usually presents with normal or high ferritin and low TIBC.
Sideroblastic anemia is also microcytic but characterized by increased iron stores and ring sideroblasts in bone marrow.

questions.explanation: The patient presents with classic symptoms of anemia and laboratory findings of microcytic hypochromic anemia. The very low serum ferritin and high TIBC are pathognomonic for iron deficiency anemia.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 68-year-old strict vegetarian male complains of progressive weakness, tingling sensation in his feet, and difficulty with balance for the past 6 months. His CBC shows Hb 9.2 g/dL, MCV 112 fL, and a peripheral blood smear shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test?

options.explanation: While folate deficiency can also cause macrocytic anemia and glossitis, it typically does not cause neurological symptoms.
The most direct initial diagnostic test is a serum Vitamin B12 level.
Reticulocyte count is not specific for diagnosing Vitamin B12 deficiency.
Bone marrow biopsy is not the initial diagnostic test for Vitamin B12 deficiency.

questions.explanation: The clinical picture of a strict vegetarian with macrocytic anemia, neurological symptoms, and glossitis is highly suggestive of Vitamin B12 deficiency.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 28-year-old man from the Mediterranean region presents for a routine check-up. He reports no specific complaints, but his CBC shows Hb 11.5 g/dL, MCV 68 fL, MCH 20 pg, and RBC count 5.8 x 10^12/L. Iron studies are all within normal limits. His Mentzer index is calculated to be 11.7. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Iron deficiency anemia would typically have low iron studies and a Mentzer index >13.
The patient's presentation and lab findings are characteristic of beta thalassemia minor.
Anemia of chronic disease would typically have abnormal iron studies and other signs of chronic disease.
Sideroblastic anemia would typically have increased iron stores and ring sideroblasts in bone marrow.

questions.explanation: The patient has microcytic hypochromic anemia with a relatively mild reduction in hemoglobin, normal iron studies, and an elevated red blood cell count, which is characteristic of thalassemia trait.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A peripheral blood smear from a 10-year-old child presenting with jaundice, pallor, and splenomegaly shows numerous small, dense, spherical red blood cells lacking central pallor. The child's parents report a family history of similar symptoms. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Iron deficiency anemia does not typically cause spherocytes.
Megaloblastic anemia does not typically cause spherocytes.
The patient's presentation and lab findings are characteristic of hereditary spherocytosis.
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia can cause spherocytes but is typically acquired and may not have a clear family history.

questions.explanation: The description of small, dense, spherical red blood cells lacking central pallor in a patient with jaundice, pallor, splenomegaly, and a family history strongly points towards hereditary spherocytosis.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 45-year-old female develops acute onset pallor, dark urine, and fatigue after starting a new antibiotic for a urinary tract infection. Her laboratory tests show Hb 7.8 g/dL, reticulocyte count 10%, elevated indirect bilirubin, and low haptoglobin. A direct Coombs test is positive. What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.explanation: While blood transfusion may be necessary for severe anemia, addressing the underlying cause is primary.

options.text: Discontinue the offending antibiotic and initiate corticosteroids
options.explanation: The most crucial initial steps are to discontinue the suspected offending drug and initiate corticosteroids to suppress the autoimmune destruction of red blood cells.
Bone marrow aspiration is not indicated in this scenario.
Iron supplementation is not indicated in this scenario.

questions.explanation: The patient presents with signs of acute hemolytic anemia and a positive direct Coombs test, indicating an autoimmune etiology.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 70-year-old male with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis presents with worsening fatigue. His CBC shows Hb 9.8 g/dL, MCV 88 fL, MCH 29 pg. Laboratory investigations reveal serum iron 35 mcg/dL, TIBC 200 mcg/dL, and serum ferritin 350 ng/mL. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Iron deficiency anemia would typically have low ferritin.
Beta thalassemia minor would typically have microcytic hypochromic anemia and normal iron studies.
The patient's presentation and lab findings are characteristic of anemia of chronic disease.
Sideroblastic anemia would typically have increased iron stores and ring sideroblasts in bone marrow.

questions.explanation: The patient has normocytic, normochromic anemia in the context of a chronic inflammatory condition, with low serum iron, low TIBC, and significantly elevated serum ferritin.

questions.question: A 55-year-old male presents with progressive fatigue, recurrent infections, and easy bruising. His CBC shows Hb 6.5 g/dL, WBC 1.5 x 10^9/L, and platelet count 20 x 10^9/L. Physical examination is unremarkable except for pallor and petechiae. A bone marrow aspiration reveals a 'dry tap,' and subsequent biopsy shows severely hypocellular marrow with increased fat content. Splenomegaly is absent. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Acute myeloid leukemia would typically have a hypercellular bone marrow.
Myelofibrosis would typically have a bone marrow biopsy showing fibrosis and a 'dry tap' due to fibrosis, not hypocellularity.
Myelodysplastic syndrome would typically have a bone marrow biopsy showing dysplastic changes and a cellular marrow.
The patient's presentation and bone marrow biopsy findings are characteristic of severe aplastic anemia.

questions.explanation: The patient presents with pancytopenia, clinical manifestations consistent with bone marrow failure, and a bone marrow biopsy showing severely hypocellular marrow.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 35-year-old female presents with progressive fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and pica. Her complete blood count reveals Hb 8.5 g/dL, MCV 72 fL, MCH 22 pg, and MCHC 28 g/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Thalassemia trait also causes microcytic anemia but typically has a normal or elevated red cell count and often a normal RDW, and pica is not a characteristic symptom.
Anemia of chronic disease is typically normocytic or mildly microcytic, and sideroblastic anemia is characterized by ring sideroblasts in the bone marrow.
The patient's symptoms (fatigue, dyspnea, pica) along with microcytic (MCV < 80 fL) and hypochromic (MCH < 27 pg, MCHC < 32 g/dL) anemia are classic findings of iron deficiency anemia.
Sideroblastic anemia is characterized by ring sideroblasts in the bone marrow.

questions.explanation: The patient's symptoms (fatigue, dyspnea, pica) along with microcytic (MCV < 80 fL) and hypochromic (MCH < 27 pg, MCHC < 32 g/dL) anemia are classic findings of iron deficiency anemia.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 68-year-old male presents with progressive fatigue, glossitis, and numbness and tingling in his feet for the past 6 months. Lab investigations show Hb 9.0 g/dL, MCV 112 fL, WBC 3.5 x 10^9/L, and Platelets 120 x 10^9/L. Serum folate is reported as normal. Which of the following additional findings would most strongly support the suspected diagnosis?

options.explanation: Increased ferritin is not characteristic of vitamin B12 deficiency.
Normal MMA would argue against B12 deficiency.
Elevated homocysteine levels are consistent with B12 deficiency and, combined with normal folate, strongly support it.
A positive direct Coombs test indicates autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which is not suggested here.

questions.explanation: The clinical picture of macrocytic anemia (MCV 112 fL) with pancytopenia, glossitis, and neurological symptoms (numbness/tingling) strongly suggests vitamin B12 deficiency.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 22-year-old male presents with worsening fatigue, recurrent epistaxis, and oral ulcers for the past several weeks. His CBC shows Hb 6.0 g/dL, MCV 90 fL, WBC 1.2 x 10^9/L (absolute neutrophil count 0.3 x 10^9/L), and Platelets 15 x 10^9/L. A peripheral blood smear reveals normocytic, normochromic red blood cells with severe panleukopenia and thrombocytopenia, but no abnormal cells or blasts are seen. The most appropriate next diagnostic step is:

options.explanation: Iron studies are less specific for this presentation.
Reticulocyte count is less specific for this presentation.

Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy are essential to confirm the diagnosis by demonstrating hypocellularity and to rule out other causes of pancytopenia like myelodysplastic syndromes or acute leukemia.
Hemoglobin electrophoresis is less specific for this presentation.

questions.explanation: The patient presents with severe pancytopenia (anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia) and a normocytic, normochromic anemia.

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy presents with a history of recurrent jaundice, splenomegaly, and cholelithiasis requiring cholecystectomy at age 8. His peripheral blood smear reveals numerous small, dense red blood cells lacking central pallor. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: G6PD deficiency causes episodic hemolysis with bite cells and Heinz bodies.
Sickle cell anemia is characterized by sickle cells.

The classic triad of recurrent jaundice, splenomegaly, and gallstones (due to chronic hemolysis) in a child, combined with the presence of spherocytes (small, dense red cells lacking central pallor) on the peripheral blood smear, is highly characteristic of hereditary spherocytosis.
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia often presents with spherocytes but is acquired and typically has a positive direct Coombs test.

questions.explanation: The classic triad of recurrent jaundice, splenomegaly, and gallstones (due to chronic hemolysis) in a child, combined with the presence of spherocytes (small, dense red cells lacking central pallor) on the peripheral blood smear, is highly characteristic of hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.question: What is the first-line treatment for uncomplicated iron deficiency anemia in an adult?

options.explanation: Parenteral iron is reserved for cases of malabsorption, intolerance to oral iron, or severe, ongoing blood loss where oral iron is insufficient.
Oral iron supplementation, typically with ferrous sulfate, is the most effective, safest, and cost-efficient first-line treatment for uncomplicated iron deficiency anemia.
Blood transfusion is not a first-line treatment for uncomplicated iron deficiency anemia.
Erythropoietin-stimulating agents are not a first-line treatment for uncomplicated iron deficiency anemia.

questions.explanation: Oral iron supplementation, typically with ferrous sulfate, is the most effective, safest, and cost-efficient first-line treatment for uncomplicated iron deficiency anemia.

questions.question: A 28-year-old male presents with fatigue and exertional dyspnea. His complete blood count reveals Hb 9.5 g/dL, MCV 72 fL, MCH 24 pg, MCHC 30 g/dL. Iron studies show serum iron 30 µg/dL, TIBC 450 µg/dL, and serum ferritin 8 ng/mL. He denies any significant bleeding. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Anemia of Chronic Disease typically has low serum iron, low TIBC, and normal or elevated ferritin.
The iron studies are classic for IDA: low serum iron, high TIBC, and very low serum ferritin.
Beta Thalassemia Minor would show microcytic anemia with normal or elevated iron studies and likely a higher RBC count.
Sideroblastic anemia is characterized by high serum iron and ferritin, with a low TIBC.

questions.explanation: The patient presents with microcytic hypochromic anemia and iron studies classic for Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA): low serum iron, high TIBC, and very low serum ferritin.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: Which of the following findings is most characteristic of megaloblastic anemia due to Vitamin B12 deficiency, as opposed to folate deficiency?

options.explanation: While both Vitamin B12 and folate deficiencies cause glossitis, it is not the most characteristic finding for Vitamin B12 deficiency.
Peripheral neuropathy is more common and severe in Vitamin B12 deficiency but is not the most specific finding.
Elevated MMA is the most characteristic finding for Vitamin B12 deficiency, as Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for the enzyme methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.
Both Vitamin B12 and folate deficiencies lead to macrocytic red blood cells, so this is not specific to Vitamin B12 deficiency.

questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anemia and can present with glossitis, peripheral neuropathy, and elevated methylmalonic acid (MMA).
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman, originally from the Mediterranean region, presents for a routine check-up. She has a lifelong history of mild anemia. Her CBC shows Hb 10.8 g/dL, MCV 68 fL, MCH 22 pg, and RBC count 5.8 x 10^12/L. Her iron studies are all within normal limits. Peripheral blood smear shows microcytosis and target cells. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

options.explanation: Bone marrow biopsy is too invasive for initial diagnosis in this scenario.
Serum erythropoietin is not indicated in this scenario.
HFE hemochromatosis causes iron overload, not microcytic anemia.
Hemoglobin electrophoresis is the definitive test to differentiate between different hemoglobinopathies by quantifying HbA, HbA2, and HbF.

questions.explanation: The patient presents with microcytic anemia, a high RBC count, and normal iron studies, suggesting a thalassemia syndrome, most likely Beta Thalassemia Minor.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A peripheral blood smear from a 4-year-old child with a recent viral infection and sudden onset pallor shows numerous small, dense, hyperchromic red blood cells lacking central pallor. There is also evidence of reticulocytosis. Which of the following conditions is most consistent with these findings?

options.explanation: Iron deficiency anemia causes microcytic, hypochromic cells, not spherocytes.
G6PD deficiency causes intravascular hemolysis with Heinz bodies and 'bite cells', not spherocytes primarily.
Hereditary Spherocytosis is characterized by spherocyte formation and chronic extravascular hemolysis, often exacerbated by viral infections.
AIHA can also cause spherocytes, but it's typically an acquired condition and often presents with a positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT).

questions.explanation: The description of small, dense, hyperchromic red blood cells lacking central pallor is classic for spherocytes, indicating Hereditary Spherocytosis.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 62-year-old male with a history of chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage IV presents with worsening fatigue. His lab results show Hb 8.9 g/dL, MCV 88 fL, MCH 29 pg. Iron studies reveal serum iron 40 µg/dL, TIBC 200 µg/dL, and serum ferritin 350 ng/mL. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his anemia?

options.explanation: Iron Deficiency Anemia would show low serum iron, high TIBC, and very low ferritin.
Beta Thalassemia Minor is microcytic with normal iron studies.
The pattern of low iron, low TIBC, and normal to high ferritin is characteristic of ACD, where inflammation leads to iron sequestration within macrophages.
Sideroblastic anemia typically has high serum iron and ferritin.

questions.explanation: The patient has normocytic, normochromic anemia with low serum iron, low TIBC, and elevated serum ferritin, characteristic of Anemia of Chronic Disease (ACD).
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the pathophysiology of Anemia of Chronic Disease (ACD) is TRUE?

options.text: There is impaired absorption of dietary iron due to primary gastrointestinal pathology.
options.explanation: Impaired absorption due to GI pathology is characteristic of IDA, not ACD.

options.text: The bone marrow fails to produce red blood cells due to aplasia.
options.explanation: Bone marrow aplasia causes aplastic anemia, not ACD.

options.text: Hepcidin levels are elevated, leading to iron sequestration in macrophages and decreased iron release from enterocytes.
options.explanation: Elevated hepcidin levels lead to the degradation of ferroportin, an iron exporter protein, on macrophages and duodenal enterocytes, causing iron sequestration and decreased iron absorption.

options.text: There is premature destruction of red blood cells in the peripheral circulation.
options.explanation: Premature destruction of red blood cells is characteristic of hemolytic anemias, not ACD.

questions.explanation: Anemia of Chronic Disease is primarily driven by inflammation leading to hepcidin elevation, causing iron sequestration in macrophages and decreased iron release from enterocytes.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 50-year-old male with a history of alcohol abuse presents with progressive fatigue and dyspnea. His CBC shows Hb 7.8 g/dL, MCV 108 fL, WBC 3,200/µL, Platelets 80,000/µL. Peripheral blood smear reveals macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils, and occasional Howell-Jolly bodies. His serum B12 level is normal. Folate level is also normal. Further investigation reveals ring sideroblasts on bone marrow biopsy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anemia but would have low serum B12 levels.
Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anemia but would have low serum folate levels.
Myelodysplastic Syndrome can present with similar findings, but Acquired Sideroblastic Anemia is a more precise fit given the information.
The history of alcohol abuse and the finding of ring sideroblasts on bone marrow biopsy strongly point towards Acquired Sideroblastic Anemia.

questions.explanation: The patient has pancytopenia and macrocytosis with megaloblastic features but normal B12 and folate levels, and ring sideroblasts on bone marrow biopsy, indicating Acquired Sideroblastic Anemia.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 25-year-old male with known G6PD deficiency develops dark urine, jaundice, and severe back pain after starting a new antimalarial drug. His Hb drops from 13 g/dL to 8 g/dL within 24 hours. Labs show elevated indirect bilirubin and LDH, with undetectable haptoglobin. His reticulocyte count is 15%. What is the most urgent next step in management?

options.explanation: Oral iron is not urgent in an acute crisis.
Folic acid might be considered for chronic hemolysis later, not as an urgent step.

options.text: Discontinue the offending drug and provide supportive care, including potential blood transfusion
options.explanation: Discontinuing the offending drug and providing supportive care, including monitoring for renal failure and potential blood transfusion, is crucial.
Corticosteroids are used in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, not G6PD deficiency.

questions.explanation: The patient is experiencing an acute hemolytic crisis triggered by an oxidizing drug in the setting of G6PD deficiency. The most urgent step is to discontinue the offending drug and provide supportive care.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 40-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, dark urine, and fatigue. His labs show Hb 9.2 g/dL, reticulocytes 10%, elevated LDH, and low haptoglobin. Flow cytometry reveals absence of CD55 and CD59 on red blood cells. Which of the following complications is he at highest risk for?

options.explanation: Megaloblastic anemia is not directly related to PNH.
While chronic hemolysis can lead to iron overload, it's not the most immediate risk.
Thrombosis is the most specific and life-threatening complication associated with the underlying pathology of PNH.
While PNH can evolve into aplastic anemia or MDS/AML, thrombosis is the most immediate and common serious complication.

questions.explanation: The patient has Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH) confirmed by flow cytometry showing absence of GPI-anchored proteins like CD55 and CD59 on red blood cells. PNH patients have a significantly increased risk of thrombosis.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy presents with pallor and easy fatigability. His parents are healthy and deny any significant family history of anemia. His CBC shows Hb 7.5 g/dL, MCV 65 fL, MCH 21 pg. Iron studies are normal. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows HbA 95%, HbA2 3.5%, HbF 1.5%. Genetic testing reveals a deletion involving one alpha-globin gene. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Beta Thalassemia Minor would show elevated HbA2.
Iron deficiency anemia would have low serum iron, high TIBC, and very low ferritin.
Alpha Thalassemia Silent Carrier typically has a milder presentation than what is described.
The severity of anemia and the genetic findings are more consistent with Alpha Thalassemia Minor, indicating a two-gene deletion.

questions.explanation: The patient presents with microcytic hypochromic anemia and normal iron studies, with hemoglobin electrophoresis showing normal HbA2 and HbF levels, characteristic of alpha-thalassemia. The genetic test revealing a deletion involving one alpha-globin gene indicates Alpha Thalassemia Trait (Silent Carrier), but the severity of anemia suggests a more significant deletion, likely Alpha Thalassemia Minor (Two-gene deletion).
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 32-year-old male presents with fatigue, pallor, and jaundice. On examination, he has splenomegaly and a palpable mass under the left costal margin. Laboratory investigations reveal: Hb: 8.2 g/dL, MCV: 88 fL, MCHC: 38 g/dL, Peripheral smear: Spherocytes, Reticulocyte count: 8%, Direct Coombs test: Positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Thalassemia major presents with microcytic anemia and target cells, while AIHA is characterized by spherocytes and a positive Coombs test.
Hereditary spherocytosis also shows spherocytes but is Coombs-negative.
The combination of spherocytes, elevated MCHC, positive direct Coombs test, and reticulocytosis is diagnostic of AIHA.
G6PD deficiency typically causes episodic hemolysis triggered by oxidative stress, not chronic hemolysis as seen in AIHA.

questions.explanation: The combination of spherocytes on peripheral smear, elevated MCHC, positive direct Coombs test, and reticulocytosis suggests autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA).
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 25-year-old female with a history of menorrhagia presents with easy bruising and gum bleeding. Lab findings: Hb: 9.5 g/dL, MCV: 68 fL, Platelet count: 250,000/µL, PT: 12 sec (normal), APTT: 38 sec (prolonged), Serum ferritin: 5 ng/mL, Peripheral smear: Microcytic hypochromic RBCs. Which additional test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

options.explanation: Hemoglobin electrophoresis is useful for diagnosing thalassemia or sickle cell disease, not for vWD.
Factor VIII may be normal or mildly reduced in vWD, but it is not the most specific test for diagnosis.
Bone marrow aspiration is not a first-line test for diagnosing vWD or iron deficiency anemia.

options.text: von Willebrand factor (vWF) antigen and activity
options.explanation: The combination of iron deficiency anemia and prolonged APTT suggests vWD, which can be confirmed by measuring vWF antigen and activity.

questions.explanation: The patient has iron deficiency anemia with menorrhagia as a likely cause. However, the prolonged APTT suggests an associated bleeding disorder, likely von Willebrand disease (vWD).
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the ER with fever and lethargy. On examination, he has pallor, petechiae, and hepatosplenomegaly. Lab results: Hb: 6.8 g/dL, WBC: 25,000/µL (80% blasts), Platelet count: 30,000/µL, Peripheral smear: Large blasts with high N:C ratio, Bone marrow: >90% blasts, PAS-positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: The combination of age, blast morphology, and PAS positivity is diagnostic of ALL.
AML is less likely in this age group and typically shows peroxidase-positive blasts.
CML presents with a leukocytosis and Philadelphia chromosome, not seen in this case.
Aplastic anemia lacks blasts and typically presents with pancytopenia and a hypocellular marrow.

questions.explanation: The child’s age, blast morphology, PAS positivity, and pancytopenia are classic for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 60-year-old male presents with progressive fatigue and shortness of breath. Lab findings: Hb: 10.2 g/dL, MCV: 110 fL, MCHC: 33 g/dL, Reticulocyte count: 1.2%, Serum B12: 200 pg/mL (normal: 200–900), Serum folate: 12 ng/mL (normal: 2–20), Peripheral smear: Hypersegmented neutrophils. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?

options.explanation: Pernicious anemia is a form of B12 deficiency but typically presents with severe B12 deficiency, which is not evident here.
Dietary folate deficiency is less likely given the patient’s age and lack of dietary history.
The patient’s age and lack of dietary history make malabsorption syndrome more likely than dietary deficiency.
Chronic alcoholism can cause macrocytosis but often with normal B12/folate levels.

questions.explanation: The macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils suggests megaloblastic anemia, likely due to malabsorption syndrome given the patient’s age and lack of dietary history.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 30-year-old female presents with recurrent episodes of dark urine, especially after infections. Lab findings: Hb: 9.8 g/dL, MCV: 90 fL, Reticulocyte count: 6%, Indirect bilirubin: 3.2 mg/dL, LDH: 450 U/L, Haptoglobin: 10 mg/dL (low), Peripheral smear: Spherocytes and fragmented RBCs. Which of the following tests is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

options.explanation: The osmotic fragility test is diagnostic for HS by showing increased RBC fragility in hypotonic solutions.
Hemoglobin electrophoresis is useful for diagnosing thalassemia or sickle cell disease, not for HS.
G6PD assay is useful for diagnosing G6PD deficiency, not for HS.
Direct Coombs test is useful for diagnosing autoimmune hemolytic anemia, not for HS.

questions.explanation: The recurrent hemolysis, low haptoglobin, elevated LDH, and spherocytes/fragmented RBCs suggest hereditary spherocytosis (HS).
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 55-year-old male with a history of chronic liver disease presents with progressive fatigue. Lab findings: Hb: 11.5 g/dL, MCV: 105 fL, Platelet count: 120,000/µL, Peripheral smear: Target cells and macrocytes, Iron studies: Ferritin 500 ng/mL, TIBC 200 µg/dL, % saturation 60%. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Iron deficiency is unlikely given the high ferritin and chronic liver disease context.
Anemia of chronic disease typically presents with normocytic or microcytic anemia, not macrocytic anemia.
Thalassemia intermedia is less likely without a family history or characteristic electrophoresis.
The combination of macrocytosis, target cells, and thrombocytopenia in a patient with chronic liver disease is diagnostic of alcohol-related macrocytic anemia.

questions.explanation: The macrocytosis with target cells and thrombocytopenia in a patient with chronic liver disease strongly suggests alcohol-related macrocytic anemia.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 22-year-old female presents with fatigue and dyspnea on exertion. Lab findings: Hb: 7.5 g/dL, MCV: 70 fL, MCHC: 30 g/dL, Reticulocyte count: 2%, Serum iron: 15 µg/dL (low), TIBC: 450 µg/dL (high), Ferritin: 8 ng/mL (low), Peripheral smear: Microcytic hypochromic RBCs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Beta-thalassemia trait presents with normal or high RBC count and characteristic hemoglobin electrophoresis.
The combination of microcytic hypochromic anemia, low ferritin, high TIBC, and low serum iron is diagnostic of IDA.
Anemia of chronic disease typically shows low TIBC and normal or high ferritin.
Sideroblastic anemia is a normocytic or macrocytic anemia with ringed sideroblasts in the marrow.

questions.explanation: The microcytic hypochromic anemia with low ferritin, high TIBC, and low serum iron is diagnostic of iron deficiency anemia (IDA).
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 6-month-old infant is brought with failure to thrive and pallor. Lab findings: Hb: 6.2 g/dL, MCV: 58 fL, Reticulocyte count: 0.5%, Peripheral smear: Microcytic hypochromic RBCs with target cells, HbA2: 5.2% (elevated), HbF: 30% (elevated). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Iron deficiency is less likely given the age and elevated HbA2.
The combination of severe microcytic hypochromic anemia, elevated HbA2, and elevated HbF is diagnostic of beta-thalassemia major.
Alpha-thalassemia trait typically shows normal HbA2.
Hemoglobin E disease presents with microcytosis and target cells but normal or mildly elevated HbF.

questions.explanation: The severe microcytic hypochromic anemia with elevated HbA2 and HbF is diagnostic of beta-thalassemia major.
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 35-year-old male presents with fever, chills, and dark urine after starting a new medication for hypertension. Lab findings: Hb: 10.5 g/dL, MCV: 85 fL, Reticulocyte count: 3%, Indirect bilirubin: 2.8 mg/dL, LDH: 380 U/L, Haptoglobin: 5 mg/dL (low), Peripheral smear: Heinz bodies on supravital stain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is characterized by a positive Coombs test, not Heinz bodies.
The combination of hemolysis triggered by oxidative stress and Heinz bodies on smear is diagnostic of G6PD deficiency.
Hereditary spherocytosis is characterized by spherocytes on smear, not Heinz bodies.
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria typically presents with hemoglobinuria and is diagnosed by flow cytometry.

questions.explanation: The hemolysis triggered by a new medication (oxidative stress) with Heinz bodies on smear is classic for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PD deficiency).
questions.subject: neet-pg-medicine

questions.question: A 70-year-old male presents with fatigue and weight loss. Lab findings: Hb: 11.8 g/dL, MCV: 102 fL, WBC: 3,200/µL, Platelet count: 90,000/µL, Peripheral smear: Dimorphic RBCs (microcytes and macrocytes), Bone marrow: Ringed sideroblasts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: The combination of dimorphic RBCs, bicytopenia, and ringed sideroblasts is diagnostic of MDS.
Vitamin B12 deficiency typically shows macrocytosis alone, not dimorphic RBCs.
Alcohol-related anemia may show macrocytosis with thrombocytopenia, but not dimorphic RBCs.
